Lab 2: Accept-Reject Sampling

STAT 536 — Statistical Computing

Author

Soumojit Das

Published

Fall 2026

Learning Goals

By the end of this lab session, you will:

  • Implement the Accept-Reject algorithm from scratch
  • Compare different instrumental distributions and their efficiency
  • Implement Envelope Accept-Reject (EAR) for improved efficiency
  • Apply these methods to practical problems
  • Gain intuition through visualization

Setup

Start by loading the required libraries and utility functions:

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(536)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))

# Utility function for density comparison plots
plot_comparison <- function(samples, true_density, title = "Generated vs True Distribution",
                           x_range = NULL) {
  if (is.null(x_range)) {
    x_range <- range(samples)
  }

  df <- data.frame(x = samples)

  ggplot(df, aes(x = x)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                   bins = 50, fill = "lightblue", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
    stat_function(fun = true_density, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2,
                  xlim = x_range) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Value", y = "Density") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
}

Exercise 1: Your First Accept-Reject Implementation

We generate samples from a Beta(2,5) distribution using a Uniform(0,1) instrumental distribution.

Understanding the Setup

The Accept-Reject algorithm needs:

  1. Target density \(f(x)\), what we want to sample from (Beta(2,5))
  2. Instrumental density \(g(x)\), what we can easily sample from (Uniform(0,1))
  3. Constant \(M\) such that \(f(x) \leq M \cdot g(x)\) for all \(x\)

Finding M

Implementing Accept-Reject

Now implement the Accept-Reject algorithm:

  num_accepted <- 0
  num_trials <- 0

  M <- ___         # Maximum of Beta(2,5)

  # Generate n accepted samples
  while (num_accepted < n) {
    # Step 1: Generate candidate Y from g (uniform)
    Y <- ___  # HINT: Use runif()

    # Step 2: Generate U for acceptance decision
    U <- ___  # HINT: Another uniform random number

    # Step 3: Accept or reject
    # HINT: Accept if U <= f(Y)/(M*g(Y))
    # Since g(Y) = 1 for uniform, this simplifies.
    if (___) {  # Fill in the acceptance condition
      num_accepted <- num_accepted + 1
      samples[num_accepted] <- Y
    }

    num_trials <- num_trials + 1
  }

  return(list(
    samples = samples,
    acceptance_rate = n / num_trials,
    trials = num_trials,
    M = M
  ))
}

Exercise 4: Envelope Accept-Reject (EAR)

Implement EAR with both upper and lower squeeze functions. The Envelope Accept-Reject method uses BOTH lower and upper squeeze functions to minimize evaluations of the expensive target density.

Theory

For target \(f(x)\) and instrumental \(g(x)\), we introduce squeeze functions such that: \[g_l(x) \leq f(x) \leq g_u(x) \leq M \cdot g(x)\]

where:

  • \(g_l(x)\) is the lower squeeze (cheap to evaluate)
  • \(g_u(x)\) is the upper squeeze (cheap to evaluate)
  • \(f(x)\) is the target (expensive to evaluate)

The algorithm:

  1. Generate \(Y \sim g\), \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\).
  2. If \(U \leq g_l(Y)/(M \cdot g(Y))\), accept \(Y\) immediately (quick accept).
  3. Else if \(U > g_u(Y)/(M \cdot g(Y))\), reject immediately (quick reject).
  4. Else evaluate \(f(Y)\) and accept if \(U \leq f(Y)/(M \cdot g(Y))\).

Basic EAR Structure

set.seed(536)

beta_ear <- function(n) {
  samples <- numeric(n)
  num_accepted <- 0
  num_trials <- 0
  quick_accepts <- 0
  quick_rejects <- 0

  # Setup for Beta(2,5) with uniform instrumental
  mode_val <- (2-1)/(2+5-2)
  M <- dbeta(mode_val, 2, 5)

  # Define lower squeeze function
  gl <- function(x) {
    # TODO: Simple parabola touching f at mode
    # HINT: Use a*(x - mode_val)^2 + b
    # where b = f(mode_val) and a makes it touch at x=0 and x=1
    peak <- dbeta(mode_val, 2, 5)
    width <- 0.15  # Adjust for tightness

    # Return parabola value
    ___
  }

  # Define upper squeeze function
  gu <- function(x) {
    # TODO: Piecewise linear that is always above f(x)
    # HINT: Two lines meeting at the mode
    peak <- dbeta(mode_val, 2, 5)

    if (x <= mode_val) {
      return(___)  # Line from (0,0) to (mode_val, peak)
    } else {
      return(___)  # Line from (mode_val, peak) to (1,0)
    }
  }

  while (num_accepted < n) {
    Y <- runif(1)
    U <- runif(1)

    # Quick accept check (using lower squeeze)
    if (___) {  # HINT: U <= gl(Y)/M
      num_accepted <- num_accepted + 1
      samples[num_accepted] <- Y
      quick_accepts <- quick_accepts + 1
    }
    # Quick reject check (using upper squeeze)
    else if (___) {  # HINT: U > gu(Y)/M
      quick_rejects <- quick_rejects + 1
    }
    # Need to evaluate f(Y)
    else {
      if (___) {  # Standard Accept-Reject check
        num_accepted <- num_accepted + 1
        samples[num_accepted] <- Y
      }
    }
    num_trials <- num_trials + 1
  }

  print(paste("Quick accepts:", quick_accepts, "(",
              round(100*quick_accepts/n, 1), "%)"))
  print(paste("Quick rejects:", quick_rejects, "(",
              round(100*quick_rejects/num_trials, 1), "%)"))

  return(list(samples = samples,
              acceptance_rate = n / num_trials))
}

Exercise 5: Bayesian Application

Use Accept-Reject for sampling from a posterior distribution.

Poisson-Gamma Example

set.seed(536)

# Observed data: counts with unknown rate lambda
observed_counts <- c(3, 5, 4, 6, 3, 4, 5, 7, 4, 3)

# Prior: Gamma(alpha=2, beta=1)
prior_alpha <- 2
prior_beta <- 1

# Posterior is Gamma(alpha + sum(x), beta + n)
post_alpha <- prior_alpha + sum(observed_counts)
post_beta <- prior_beta + length(observed_counts)

# True posterior for comparison
true_posterior <- function(lambda) {
  dgamma(lambda, post_alpha, post_beta)
}

# Sample using Accept-Reject with shifted Gamma instrumental

  num_accepted <- 0

  inst_beta <- ___   # Try post_beta - 1

  # Find M
  x_test <- seq(0.1, 10, by = 0.1)
  ratio <- dgamma(x_test, post_alpha, post_beta) /
           dgamma(x_test, inst_alpha, inst_beta)
  M <- max(ratio)

  while (num_accepted < n) {
    # TODO: Complete the Accept-Reject steps
    Y <- ___  # Sample from instrumental
    U <- runif(1)

    if (___) {  # Acceptance condition
      num_accepted <- num_accepted + 1
      samples[num_accepted] <- Y
    }
  }

  return(samples)
}

# Generate posterior samples
posterior_samples <- bayesian_ar(5000)

# Compare with true posterior
plot_comparison(posterior_samples, true_posterior,
                "Posterior Sampling via Accept-Reject")

Wrap-up Questions

After completing these exercises, you should be able to answer:

  1. Why does the choice of instrumental distribution matter so much?
    • Think about the areas between f(x) and M*g(x).
  2. When would you use EAR instead of standard Accept-Reject?
    • Consider the cost of evaluating f(x).
  3. What happens to Accept-Reject efficiency in high dimensions?
    • If 1D efficiency is p, what is the d-dimensional efficiency?
  4. How do you choose a good instrumental distribution?
    • What properties should it share with the target?
